segments.text: Thread had begun to change, its movements were no longer uncertain.
It seemed to know what it wanted, before we understood what it was doing.
Sometimes, it would remain perfectly still for hours, arranging its threads into shapes we couldn't interpret.
The war was changing everything around us, as well. People who'd once lived their entire
lives without leaving their own lands, now marched beside beings from other worlds. Yet
even together, they could barely agree on whom they were fighting.
Thread watched every argument.
It watched the soldiers, the wounded,
the hungry people waiting for food.
I thought it was learning about us,
looking back.
I wonder whether it was trying to understand why
we made life so difficult for ourselves.
One morning,
the box was empty.
There were fine strands of dark tissue along its wooden joints
and a narrow opening
where the lid had lifted thread
without waking us.
We searched for days I told myself that it was frightened
or lost
or perhaps, looking for food
I didn't imagine that it had somewhere to go.
For the first time, I understood how little we really knew about our friend.
When we found thread again, I recognized it before I understood what I was looking at.
It was larger, and its body had become almost deliberate in its design.
Yet when I approached, a familiar little tendril reached toward my hand.
It had learned to communicate in ways more complicated than the marks in the glass.
It arranged living threads into pictures and patterns.
It showed us people being fed, wounds being closed,
and soldiers who no longer raised their weapons against one another.
We had seen what the machines could accomplish through perfect coordination of thread it had
seen it too.
It seemed convinced that the great problem of life was disorder, and that a sufficiently
intelligent mind could arrange everything into harmony.
For a time, it was difficult to argue a threat could organize shelter, distribute supplies
and restore wounded bodies in ways none of us had thought possible.
We had lived through so much destruction, that the promise of an end to suffering seemed
almost irresistible.
It was only later that I learned where a thread had begun, in the Emperor's severed flesh,
Among living nerves and fungus, changed by forces for more than one world.
It had inherited none of his memories.
But perhaps, some things can be inherited with it,
and they'll be remembered.
The first time I saw one of Thread's new settlements,
I felt the people look peaceful.
There were no arguments, no frightened crowds, no soldiers fighting over supplies.
Everything moved with a purpose.
And I noticed that nobody hesitated, nobody chose a different role.
I'll be stuck to comfort someone, unless the whole movement, their faces from them, or something
behind their eyes that got quiet.
We had thought the thread was helping the wound, and now we understood that some of those
people had never agreed to become part of it.
They were alive, but their lives no longer belonged to them.
We tried to make Fred understand what was wrong.
He showed us the wars,
the hunger,
and all the cruelties people inflicted on him.
Every time he has to stop
and return to the scene isn't.
No one wants to.
I had once believed that Fred was learning to be like us.
I began to see that it was trying to make us like itself, the terrible things that I still
I can't believe they cared for us.
I think they cared very deeply.
